title: MODULE 08 — React Fundamentals and Component Engineering

overview.text: Module overview

Modern frontend applications require more than JavaScript and TypeScript. Developers need a structured way to build user interfaces, organize application logic, manage changing data, and reuse components across different pages.
Imagine building a learning platform such as PrepSpaces.
The application might contain:
A navigation bar shared across every page.
Course cards displaying information from an API.
A student dashboard showing learning progress.
Interactive buttons for completing lessons.
Forms for authentication and registration.
Notifications that update when new information arrives.
Reusable components shared across multiple courses.
Building all these features using manually manipulated HTML and DOM operations can become difficult as the application grows.
React provides a component-based approach to solving this problem.
What is React?

Developed and maintained by Meta and the React community.
React allows developers to describe what the interface should look like for a particular application state.
When the state changes, React renders the component again and updates the relevant parts of the interface.
Instead of manually finding HTML elements and modifying them, developers describe the interface using components and JSX.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — Introduction to React and Component-Based Architecture

blocks.text: 1.1 The problem with traditional DOM manipulation

Suppose you want to create a counter.

sections.title: LESSON 04 — Functional Components and Component Composition

blocks.text: Functional components are JavaScript or TypeScript functions that return React elements.
Function components are the normal way to build modern React interfaces.
Instead of creating an entire dashboard in a single component, divide it into reusable parts.

function Navbar() { return (

PrepSpaces

Home Courses
); } export default Navbar;

function Footer() { return (

Learning Platform

); } export default Footer;

import Navbar from "./components/Navbar"; import Footer from "./components/Footer"; function App() { return ( <>

Student Dashboard

); } export default App;
Component composition means creating larger interfaces by combining smaller components.

App │ ├── Navbar │ ├── Dashboard │ │ │ ├── WelcomeSection │ │ │ ├── StatisticsSection │ │ ├── StatisticsCard │ │ └── StatisticsCard │ │ │ └── CourseSection │ ├── CourseCard │ ├── CourseCard │ └── CourseCard │ └── Footer
Each component has a specific responsibility.
This is usually easier to test, understand, and maintain than one extremely large component.
React supports nested composition through children.

import type { ReactNode } from "react"; interface CardProps { children: ReactNode; } function Card({ children }: CardProps) { return (
{children}
); }

function Dashboard() { return (

Learning Progress

You've completed 8 lessons.

The Card component doesn't need to know what its children contain.
It simply provides a reusable container.
4.5 Component responsibility and separation of concerns
Approach A: One component handles everything:
Approach B: Separate components and supporting functions handle individual responsibilities.
Approach B generally provides better maintainability.
However, components should not be divided into extremely tiny pieces without a meaningful reason. Good component boundaries reflect independent responsibilities and reuse.
Practical exercise: Design a student dashboard using at least eight components. Identify which components should be reused and which should remain specific to one page.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — Props and One-Way Data Flow

blocks.text: Props allow one component to pass information to another component.
Consider an application displaying three courses.
Each course card needs different information:
Instead of creating three separate components, create one reusable component and pass different props to it.

interface CourseCardProps { title: string; description: string; level: string; } function CourseCard({ title, description, level }: CourseCardProps) { return (

{title}

{description}

{level}
); }

function CourseSection() { return (
); }
The same component renders different information depending on the props it receives.
React follows a one-way data flow model for component props.
A parent component passes information to its child components.
A child receives information from its parent.
A child should not directly modify the parent's props.
Props are read-only inputs to a component.
Sometimes a child component needs to request an action from its parent.
For example, a child course card may contain an Enrol button.
The parent owns the course enrollment operation.
The child receives a callback function.

interface CourseCardProps { title: string; onEnroll: () => void; } function CourseCard({ title, onEnroll }: CourseCardProps) { return (

{title}

); }
function CourseSection() { function handleEnroll() { console.log("Student enrolled"); } return ( <CourseCard title="React" onEnroll={handleEnroll} /> ); }
The child receives the function and calls it when the user interacts with the button.
This preserves the direction of data ownership while allowing child-to-parent communication through callbacks.
Both need to work with the selected search term.
They are siblings, so neither should directly control the other.
Instead, move their shared state into a common parent.
Passes the updated value to CourseList.
This technique is called lifting state up.
React components can receive props through object spreading.
This is convenient when passing an existing object whose properties match the component's expected inputs.
Avoid unnecessary spreading of large objects because it can make component dependencies less obvious.
A component needs information from its parent.
A parent needs to control the behaviour of a child.
A reusable component should support configuration.
Children need callbacks to communicate actions upward.
Practical exercise: Build a reusable CourseCard that accepts course information, an enrollment callback, an optional image, and a publication status.
State represents information that a component remembers between renders.
When state changes, React schedules another render so the interface can reflect the new state.
React provides a Hook called useState to manage local component state.
A function that requests an update to the state.

import { useState } from "react"; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return (

Count: {count}

); }
When the user clicks the button, React receives a state update and renders the component again.
One of the most important React concepts is that state behaves like a snapshot for a particular render.
function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); function handleClick() { setCount(count + 1); console.log(count); } return ( <button onClick={handleClick}> Count: {count} </button> ); }
The console logs the value from the current render, not the updated value.
For example, when the button is clicked while the count is 0, the console logs 0.
This is because calling the setter does not change the state variable inside the already-running function.
The next render receives the updated value.
Sometimes the next value depends on the previous value.
In these situations, use a functional updater.

function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); function increaseThreeTimes() { setCount(value => value + 1); setCount(value => value + 1); setCount(value => value + 1); } return (

{count}

); }
The updater functions are processed using the previous queued value.
This correctly increases the count by three.
Using setCount(count + 1) three times in the same event handler would not achieve the same result.

interface Student { name: string; age: number; } function StudentProfile() { const [student, setStudent] = useState({ name: "Alex", age: 22 }); function updateName() { setStudent(previous => ({ ...previous, name: "Sam" })); } return (

{student.name}

{student.age}

); }
Notice the use of the spread operator.
React state should be treated as immutable.
Do not directly modify the existing object:
interface Task { id: number; title: string; completed: boolean; }
function addTask() { const newTask: Task = { id: Date.now(), title: "Learn React", completed: false }; setTasks(previous => [ ...previous, newTask ]); }
function removeTask(taskId: number) { setTasks(previous => previous.filter(task => task.id !== taskId) ); }
function completeTask(taskId: number) { setTasks(previous => previous.map(task => task.id === taskId ? { ...task, completed: true } : task ) ); }
These methods create new arrays and objects instead of mutating existing state.
Not every value needs to be stored in React state.
This value can be calculated directly from the existing state.
Avoid storing values that can be derived from other state unless there is a good reason.
Excessive duplicated state can create synchronization bugs.
Changes because of a user interaction.
Needs to be remembered between renders.
Needs to trigger an interface update when modified.
Practical exercise: Build a task list using useState. Add, edit, complete, and delete tasks. Ensure arrays and objects are updated immutably.

sections.title: LESSON 07 — Event Handling and Interactive Components

blocks.text: 7.1 What is event handling in React?
React applications respond to events generated by users and the browser.
React provides event properties through JSX.
function App() { function handleClick() { console.log("Button clicked"); } return ( <button onClick={handleClick}> Click Me </button> ); }
An event handler is a function that runs when a particular event occurs.
The second example calls the function during rendering rather than waiting for the click.
Sometimes a handler needs information about the item that was clicked.
function CourseButton() { function handleClick(courseId: number) { console.log("Selected course:", courseId); } return ( <button onClick={() => handleClick(101)}> Select Course </button> ); }
The arrow function delays the call until the event occurs.
React event handlers can receive an event object.
function SearchButton() { function handleClick( event: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement> ) { console.log(event.currentTarget); } return ( <button onClick={handleClick}> Search </button> ); }
The event object provides information about the interaction.

function SearchBox() { function handleKeyDown( event: React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement> ) { if (event.key === "Enter") { console.log("Search submitted"); } } return ( <input type="text" onKeyDown={handleKeyDown} /> ); }
This is useful for search fields, keyboard navigation, and shortcut functionality.
Browser events can propagate through the DOM.

function Parent() { return (
console.log("Parent clicked")}>
); }
Clicking the button logs the button message without triggering the parent click handler.
React's event system follows familiar event propagation concepts, though its event implementation has React-specific behaviour.

import { useState } from "react"; function LikeButton() { const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false); return ( <button onClick={() => setLiked(value => !value)} > {liked ? "Liked" : "Like"} </button> ); }
The button updates its own state and changes its interface.
Practical exercise: Build interactive React components for a like button, dropdown, modal, tab selector, and search field.

React needs a stable way to identify elements in a list.
This is why developers provide a key property.

Keys help React match list items between renders when items are inserted, deleted, or reordered.
Avoid using an array index as a key for lists whose items can move, be inserted, or be deleted. This can cause state or DOM identity to be associated with the wrong item.

sections.title: LESSON 09 — Managing Forms and User Input

blocks.text: Forms are among the most common interactive parts of frontend applications.
React offers different approaches to collecting form information.
A controlled component is a form input whose value is controlled by React state.

import { useState } from "react"; function SearchForm() { const [search, setSearch] = useState(""); return (
setSearch(event.target.value) } />

You searched for: {search}

); }
The input value is always synchronized with the state.
The input generates a change event.
The handler reads the new value.
A registration form may have several properties.

import { useState } from "react"; interface RegistrationForm { name: string; email: string; password: string; } function Registration() { const [form, setForm] = useState<RegistrationForm>({ name: "", email: "", password: "" }); function handleChange( event: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> ) { const { name, value } = event.target; setForm(previous => ({ ...previous, [name]: value })); } function handleSubmit( event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> ) { event.preventDefault(); console.log(form); } return ( <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> <input name="name" value={form.name} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Name" /> <input name="email" type="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Email" /> <input name="password" type="password" value={form.password} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Password" /> <button type="submit"> Register </button> </form> ); }
The computed property [name] updates the correct field without creating a different event handler for every input.

const [accepted, setAccepted] = useState(false);
<label> <input type="checkbox" checked={accepted} onChange={event => setAccepted(event.target.checked) } /> Accept terms and conditions </label>
For checkboxes, use checked, not value, to control whether they are selected.

const [level, setLevel] = useState("Beginner");
<select value={level} onChange={event => setLevel(event.target.value)} > <option value="Beginner">Beginner</option> <option value="Intermediate">Intermediate</option> <option value="Advanced">Advanced</option> </select>
For an uncontrolled input, React can use a ref to access its DOM element.

import { useRef } from "react"; function SearchForm() { const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null); function handleSubmit( event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> ) { event.preventDefault(); console.log(inputRef.current?.value); } return ( <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> <input ref={inputRef} /> <button type="submit"> Search </button> </form> ); }
Forms should validate information before submitting it.
Use validation for user experience, but always repeat essential validation on the backend.
Frontend validation alone cannot protect server-side data.
Practical exercise: Build a task-creation form with title, description, priority, deadline, and input validation.

sections.title: LESSON 10 — React Hooks and the Rules of Hooks

blocks.text: Hooks are functions provided by React that allow function components to use React features such as state, context, references, and effects.
This module focuses on the fundamental Hooks in your syllabus.
Earlier React development heavily used class components to manage state and lifecycle behaviour.
Hooks made it possible to use those React capabilities inside function components.
Instead of separating logic across lifecycle methods, developers can organize related logic within a component or reusable Hook.
Rule 1: Call Hooks only at the top level.

function Dashboard() { if (true) { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); } return
Dashboard
; }

function Dashboard() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return
{count}
; }
Rule 2: Call Hooks only from React functions.
They should not be called from ordinary JavaScript functions.
React relies on the order of Hook calls to associate Hook state with the correct component instance.

function Profile() { const [name, setName] = useState("Alex"); const [age, setAge] = useState(22); return

{name}, {age}

; }
React encounters the Hooks in a consistent order.
If a Hook is conditionally skipped, the order can become inconsistent across renders.
This is why Hook calls must remain at the top level.
10.6 Why Hook names start with use
Custom Hooks normally start with use.
This naming convention helps React tooling and developers recognize Hook usage.
Not every calculation needs a Hook.

function CourseProgress() { const completed = 8; const total = 10; const percentage = (completed / total) * 100; return

{percentage}%

; }
There is no need to use state or an effect for this simple calculation.
Hooks should be introduced when they provide a meaningful React capability.
Practical exercise: Identify incorrect Hook usage in sample components and rewrite those components so all Hooks follow the Rules of Hooks.

sections.title: LESSON 11 — useEffect and Synchronizing with External Systems

blocks.text: useEffect is a React Hook used to synchronize a component with something outside React.
useEffect(() => { // Synchronization logic return () => { // Cleanup logic }; }, [dependencies]);
The dependency array controls when the effect is re-synchronized.
The effect is scheduled after every commit of that component.
This effect has no reactive dependencies.
In production, it is typically set up on the initial mount, with cleanup when the component unmounts.
Development Strict Mode may perform an additional setup-and-cleanup cycle to help detect unsafe effects.
The effect is re-synchronized after commits when courseId changes.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; interface Course { id: number; title: string; } function CourseList() { const [courses, setCourses] = useState([]); const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true); const [error, setError] = useState(null); useEffect(() => { const controller = new AbortController(); async function loadCourses() { try { setLoading(true); setError(null); const response = await fetch( "/api/courses", { signal: controller.signal } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Unable to load courses"); } const data: unknown = await response.json(); if (!Array.isArray(data)) { throw new Error("Invalid course response"); } setCourses(data as Course[]); } catch (error) { if ( error instanceof Error && error.name !== "AbortError" ) { setError(error.message); } } finally { if (!controller.signal.aborted) { setLoading(false); } } } loadCourses(); return () => { controller.abort(); }; }, []); if (loading) { return

Loading courses...

; } if (error) { return

{error}

; } return (
{courses.map(course => (

{course.title}

))}
); }
For production use, replace the simple array check and type assertion with proper runtime validation, as learned in Module 07.
Some effects create resources that must be released.
useEffect(() => { const intervalId = setInterval(() => { console.log("Dashboard refresh"); }, 5000); return () => { clearInterval(intervalId); }; }, []);
When the component no longer needs the timer, the cleanup function clears it.
Suppose an application needs to know the current window width.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; function WindowWidth() { const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth); useEffect(() => { function handleResize() { setWidth(window.innerWidth); } window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize); handleResize(); return () => { window.removeEventListener( "resize", handleResize ); }; }, []); return

Width: {width}px

; }
The component subscribes to a browser event and cleans up its listener when necessary.
A common mistake is using useEffect for every calculation.

const [tasks, setTasks] = useState<Task[]>([]); const [completedCount, setCompletedCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { setCompletedCount( tasks.filter(task => task.completed).length ); }, [tasks]);
The second approach is usually preferable because the value is derived directly from existing state.
React's guidance is to use Effects for synchronization with external systems, rather than for calculations that can be performed during rendering.
Effects can sometimes use outdated values if dependencies are missing.
If courseId changes later, the effect does not re-synchronize.
Dependency arrays should reflect the reactive values used by the effect.
Practical exercise: Build an API-powered course component that retrieves information, responds to changing course IDs, handles errors, and cancels outdated requests.
useRef is a React Hook that provides a mutable reference whose value is preserved between renders.
It is commonly used for two purposes:
Storing mutable values that do not need to trigger a re-render.
The reference object contains a current property.
You want to automatically focus the input when the user clicks a button.

import { useRef } from "react"; function SearchBox() { const inputRef = useRef(null); function focusInput() { inputRef.current?.focus(); } return (
); }
useRef() creates a persistent reference object.
React attaches the input element to the reference after it is committed.
inputRef.current points to the actual DOM element.
The button handler calls the DOM element's focus() method.
This is useful when interacting with browser features that require direct DOM access.
Changing the count causes React to schedule a render.
Changing current does not cause a re-render.
A timer identifier is a useful example of a value that does not necessarily need to be displayed.

import { useRef } from "react"; function Timer() { const timerRef = useRef(null); function startTimer() { timerRef.current = window.setInterval(() => { console.log("Timer running"); }, 1000); } function stopTimer() { if (timerRef.current !== null) { window.clearInterval(timerRef.current); timerRef.current = null; } } return (
); }
A complete implementation should also clear an active timer when the component unmounts.
Refs can preserve values between renders without triggering additional renders.

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react"; function CourseTitle({ title }: { title: string }) { const previousTitle = useRef( undefined ); useEffect(() => { console.log("Previous title:", previousTitle.current); previousTitle.current = title; }, [title]); return

{title}

; }
This example records the previous title after an effect runs.
Avoid treating refs as replacements for normal React state.
If a value needs to update the interface automatically, state is normally more appropriate.
Also avoid modifying DOM elements directly when React can handle the same operation through normal rendering.
Use refs for specific integrations and imperative operations, not as the primary interface-rendering mechanism.
Practical exercise: Build a form with automatic input focusing, a timer, a scroll-to-top button, and a modal that focuses its first input when opened.

sections.title: LESSON 13 — Component Lifecycle and Rendering Behavior

blocks.text: React components go through different stages during their existence.
Traditionally, these stages are described as:
Understanding these stages helps developers manage effects, external subscriptions, timers, and component state.
Mounting means that a component is being added to the interface for the first time.
When the component is first displayed, React renders it and commits the resulting interface.
A mount-related effect can be written as:
The empty dependency array indicates that the effect has no reactive dependencies.
Remember that React Strict Mode can run an additional development-only setup and cleanup cycle.
Updating occurs when a component renders again because of changes to its inputs or state.
function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}> {count} </button> ); }
React receives the new element description.
React determines what needs to change.
Unmounting occurs when a component is removed from the rendered component tree.

function App() { const [visible, setVisible] = useState(true); return (
{visible && }
); }
Clicking the button removes the Dashboard component from the rendered tree.
An effect cleanup function is the appropriate place to release resources:

function Dashboard() { useEffect(() => { const interval = setInterval(() => { console.log("Updating dashboard"); }, 1000); return () => { clearInterval(interval); console.log("Dashboard cleanup"); }; }, []); return

Dashboard

; }
React's rendering process has two important conceptual stages.
React calls components and calculates the next interface description.
During this stage, component logic should remain pure.
React applies necessary changes to the host environment, such as updating the browser DOM.
Effects are handled according to their scheduling rules after the relevant commit.
This separation is important because a component may render more than once without every render leading to a DOM change.
A React component can render again when:
Its parent renders and React renders that child as part of the updated tree.
Other React mechanisms schedule an update.
A re-render does not necessarily mean the browser DOM is completely recreated.
React compares the resulting element descriptions and commits the updates needed to synchronize the interface.
13.7 Why React Strict Mode is important
In development, React Strict Mode performs additional checks to help reveal unsafe rendering behaviour and missing cleanup logic.
For example, an effect may undergo an extra setup-cleanup-setup cycle in development.
This is intentional development behaviour, not evidence that production users will automatically experience duplicate effect setups in the same way.
Effects should be written so that setup and cleanup correctly mirror each other.
13.8 Understanding state preservation and component identity
React associates state with a component's position and identity in the rendered tree.
For example, when the same component remains at the same position with the same identity, its state is generally preserved between renders.
Changing its key can intentionally create a different component identity.
When userId changes, the key changes, so React treats the new editor as a different component instance and resets its local state.
This can be useful when switching between different user profiles or independent editing sessions.

function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // Do not call setCount unconditionally here. return

{count}

; }
Updating state unconditionally during render can create repeated or infinite rendering.
Mistake 3: Performing network requests directly during rendering
This would start requests whenever the component renders.
Use an effect or an appropriate data-fetching approach instead.
Practical exercise: Build a component that mounts, updates, and unmounts while managing an event listener and timer. Observe its render and cleanup behaviour in development Strict Mode.

sections.title: LESSON 14 — Reusable Components and Custom Hooks

blocks.text: A reusable component is an interface element designed to be used in multiple locations without duplicating its implementation.
Consider a button used across an application.
Without a reusable component, developers might repeatedly write slightly different button markup.
A reusable component centralizes the common behaviour and design.

interface ButtonProps { children: React.ReactNode; variant?: "primary" | "secondary" | "danger"; disabled?: boolean; onClick?: () => void; } function Button({ children, variant = "primary", disabled = false, onClick }: ButtonProps) { return ( <button className={`button button-${variant}`} disabled={disabled} onClick={onClick} > {children} </button> ); }
<Button variant="primary"> Save </Button> <Button variant="secondary"> Cancel </Button> <Button variant="danger"> Delete </Button>
One implementation supports several use cases.

import type { ReactNode } from "react"; interface CardProps { title: string; children: ReactNode; } function Card({ title, children }: CardProps) { return (

{title}

{children}
); }
This card can be reused for:
The content changes, while the common structure stays consistent.
A custom Hook is a JavaScript or TypeScript function that uses React Hooks to encapsulate and reuse stateful logic.
It allows developers to separate repeated behaviour from individual components.
For example, multiple components may need to manage similar search logic.
Instead of duplicating it, developers can create one custom Hook.

import { useState } from "react"; function useToggle(initialValue = false) { const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue); function toggle() { setValue(previous => !previous); } return { value, toggle }; }

function Modal() { const { value: isOpen, toggle } = useToggle(); return (
{isOpen && (

Modal Content

)}
); }
The custom Hook can be reused by other components.
React can use a custom Hook to connect component state with LocalStorage.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; function useLocalStorage( key: string, initialValue: string ) { const [value, setValue] = useState(() => { try { const stored = localStorage.getItem(key); return stored ?? initialValue; } catch { return initialValue; } }); useEffect(() => { try { localStorage.setItem(key, value); } catch (error) { console.error("Unable to save preference", error); } }, [key, value]); return [value, setValue] as const; }

function ThemeSelector() { const [theme, setTheme] = useLocalStorage( "theme", "light" ); return ( <button onClick={() => setTheme(theme === "light" ? "dark" : "light") } > Current theme: {theme} </button> ); }
This demonstrates how custom Hooks combine state with browser-side synchronization.
For production applications, this example can be expanded to support multiple tabs, object serialization, storage failures, and server-side rendering constraints.
A custom Hook can also organize asynchronous data retrieval.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; interface FetchState<T> { data: T | null; loading: boolean; error: string | null; } function useFetch<T>(url: string) { const [state, setState] = useState<FetchState<T>>({ data: null, loading: true, error: null }); useEffect(() => { const controller = new AbortController(); async function loadData() { setState({ data: null, loading: true, error: null }); try { const response = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error( `Request failed: ${response.status}` ); } const data: unknown = await response.json(); if (!controller.signal.aborted) { // The caller must provide runtime validation // before trusting external data as T. setState({ data: data as T, loading: false, error: null }); } } catch (error) { if ( error instanceof Error && error.name !== "AbortError" && !controller.signal.aborted ) { setState({ data: null, loading: false, error: error.message }); } } } loadData(); return () => { controller.abort(); }; }, [url]); return state; }

interface Course { id: number; title: string; } function Courses() { const { data, loading, error } = useFetch("/api/courses"); if (loading) return

Loading...

; if (error) return

{error}

; return (
{data?.map(course => (

{course.title}

))}
); }

Important: Generics describe the expected data type, but they do not validate API responses. As discussed in Module 07, production implementations should validate the response with a runtime schema before treating it as T.
Called inside components or other Hooks
A custom Hook does not create shared state automatically across different components.
Each component calling the Hook normally receives its own Hook state.
Practical exercise: Build reusable Button, Card, Modal, and Input components. Then create useToggle, useLocalStorage, and useFetch custom Hooks.

sections.title: PRACTICAL PROJECT — Interactive Task Management Application

blocks.text: Project: Build a Task Management Application Using React and TypeScript
Build a fully functional task management application using React, TypeScript, and Vite.
The application should allow users to create tasks, update their information, mark tasks as completed, organize priorities, search tasks, and manage their work through an interactive interface.
This project combines the concepts learned in Modules 05–08.
